## ✦ IN A NUTSHELL

The brain index was regenerated correctly at branch head d12fcbd71 (04:46:56Z — `--check` exit 0, "OK: index layer matches git tree (1329 files)"). It drifted not because the generator broke, but because the merge (1a1c22d32, 08:09:41Z) committed those bytes onto a main tree that had advanced 3 files past the regen snapshot. Git merges file bytes; it never re-runs your generator. Version skew was ruled out first: `git log 7a6a79951..1a1c22d32 -- tools/regenerate_brain_index.py` returned zero commits — the tool is exonerated, the timing is the cause. The main side had the same bug in mirror form: three projection commits (5b6bb9298, 25ddcf2cf, f424f5b97) landed BRAIN/ files without ever regenerating. The rule: **when generated-artifact DRIFT appears, pin the timing before the tool — cite the regen commit SHA, the merge commit SHA, and the generator's commit range since last-green. Empty generator range + merge carrying older bytes = timing, not tool.** Re-running regen at the newest tip and committing is the one-line fix; the generator was never the suspect.

## 🩷 HUMAN NOTE

Shawn — evidence lesson from the verify lane: the brain-index drift that went red on main was traced to its exact cause. The index was regenerated on the branch at 04:46Z and was correct then — but the merge at 08:09Z carried those bytes onto a main that had since added 3 more files. Git merges bytes; it doesn't re-run the generator. The lane ruled out a broken generator first (zero changes to the tool in the whole window) and routed the fix: regenerate at the newest tip and commit. New lane rule: when drift shows up, check regen-time vs merge-time before blaming the tool. Filed as Smart Note candidate SN-01712.

## 🟣 CHILD NOTE

Imagine you take a perfect photo of your bookshelf. Then your mom adds 3 new books, and you tape your old photo into the catalog as the new page. The photo isn't wrong — it was perfect when you took it. The catalog is wrong because it used a photo taken before the 3 books arrived. Blaming the camera would be silly — you'd check WHEN the photo was taken first. That's the whole lesson: check the timing before you blame the tool.

## 🔵 GRANDMA NOTE

The team keeps a machine-generated index of every file in the brain. Overnight the index went stale and the tests flagged it. The investigation found the generator worked perfectly — it had made a correct index an hour earlier. The problem was the merge: it carried that correct-but-now-old index onto a newer version of the repository without refreshing it — like mailing yesterday's newspaper and calling it today's. The new rule: when the index looks wrong, first check when it was generated versus when it was merged. Don't assume the generator is broken.

## 🟠 NAYA NOTE

Diagnosis seat: a generated-artifact DRIFT verdict is incomplete unless it cites three pins: (1) the regen commit SHA and its timestamp (plus the `--check` exit code there), (2) the merge/landing commit SHA and its timestamp, (3) `git log <last_green>..<drift_tip> -- <generator_path>` — non-empty means version skew is a live suspect; empty means the tool is exonerated and timing is the cause. Run this BEFORE opening a generator bug hunt. Route the fix, never self-execute: regen at the newest tip + commit (the gate's own log prescribes it). Check both sides: the branch side (merge carrying old bytes) AND the main side (projection commits landing content without regenerating) — same bug, two venues.
